title: MaskSense: Confronting the Visual Exploration Trap in Masked Image Generation

paper.title: MaskSense: Confronting the Visual Exploration Trap in Masked Image Generation
paper.abstract:
Abstract Reinforcement learning (RL) has shown strong potential for aligning generative models with human intent, but adapting RL to masked generative models (MGMs) remains largely underexplored.
Existing approaches that directly adapt Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to MGMs leave a foundational conflict unaddressed: MGMs’ exploitative decoding nature is inherently at odds with the exploratory diversity that GRPO presupposes.
In this work, we reveal a structural decoding bias termed the visual exploration trap : confidence-based sampling trades the exploration of diverse subject realizations for the greedy resolution of low-uncertainty background regions, causing premature collapse of the generative exploration space and starving GRPO of the rollout diversity it depends on.
To this end, we propose MaskSense , a novel RL framework for MGMs that confronts the visual exploration trap at both the sampling and optimization stages. Specifically, we introduce a semantic anchored routing sampling mechanism that leverages semantic priors to preserve high-entropy subject token exploration while amplifying intra-group reward variance through exploratory-exploitative routing
to yield more discriminative advantage estimates.
Furthermore, we design a global entropy transition anchoring strategy to identify the most consequential decoding steps and concentrate gradient updates on them.
Extensive experiments on multiple text-to-image benchmarks demonstrate that MaskSense substantially improves upon the base model, with GenEval accuracy improving from 54% to 86% and HPS from 28.89 to 36.39, achieving state-of-the-art performance.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Masked generative models (MGMs) [ 1 , 5 , 63 , 15 ] have recently emerged as a compelling paradigm for visual synthesis, challenging the long-standing dominance of autoregressive models (AR) [ 57 , 24 , 48 ] and diffusion models (DMs) [ 46 , 16 , 23 ] by reformulating image generation as iterative masked token prediction. Central to this paradigm is the confidence-based sampling strategy of MaskGIT [ 6 ] , which predicts all masked tokens in parallel at each step and retains only the most confident subset while remasking the remainder for subsequent iterations, making the decoding process exploitative. Reinforcement learning (RL) [ 45 , 40 , 36 ] has proven highly effective in enhancing the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) [ 13 , 17 , 54 , 41 ] , while its application to MGMs remains comparatively underexplored relative to diffusion models [ 25 , 42 , 65 ] and AR models [ 18 , 70 ] . Recent works [ 69 , 28 ] have begun addressing this gap by applying Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to MGMs, yet retain the confidence-based sampler as a fixed component with minimal adaptation to the masked generation setting. This overlooks a fundamental prerequisite of GRPO: its effectiveness derives from group-relative advantage estimation, which presupposes rollouts sufficiently diverse to cover meaningful regions of the solution space, a requirement inherently at odds with the exploitative nature of confidence-based sampling. In this paper, we identify and characterize precisely how this conflict manifests as a structural bias that we term the visual exploration trap . Specifically, tokens with lower uncertainty predominantly correspond to simple background textures in natural images [ 30 ] , causing background regions to be committed well before semantically critical subject areas are ever explored (Fig. 1 (a)). Subject tokens, by contrast, retain high predictive entropy throughout the early generation steps, while their fixation ratio remains near zero (Fig. 1 (c)), indicating that substantial generative diversity is available yet remains entirely unexploited. By the time subject tokens begin to be retained after step 20, the surrounding background context has been largely committed, severely narrowing the space of potential generative branches [ 32 , 54 ] and limiting the diversity and quality of the resulting subject regions [ 30 ] . The originally high entropy of subject tokens is thus suppressed before any meaningful subject decision is made, as the model effectively sacrifices diverse subject realizations to greedily resolve low-uncertainty background regions, directly undermining the rollout diversity that GRPO requires. This trap necessitates a rethink of RL for MGMs. Figure 1 : Motivation. (a) MaskGIT keeps subject tokens masked while committing background regions early, whereas SA-Sampler resolves subject regions earlier via semantic anchoring. (b) SA-Sampler consistently discovers higher-reward trajectories through broader generative exploration. (c) SA-Sampler maintains higher subject-token fixation ratios and elevated entropy, effectively escaping the visual exploration trap. To tackle this challenge, we propose MaskSense (Fig. 2 ), a novel RL framework designed for MGMs that directly confronts the visual exploration trap at both the sampling and optimization stages. At the sampling stage, we propose the semantic anchored routing sampling (SARS) mechanism, built upon the Semantic Anchored Sampler (SA-Sampler), which employs semantic priors to anchor subject tokens during the early generation steps (Fig. 1 (a)). This design preserves the high-entropy exploration space that confidence-based sampling would otherwise suppress (Fig. 1 (c)), enabling the discovery of higher-reward trajectories through broader generative exploration (Fig. 1 (b)). SARS further routes rollouts stochastically between SA-Sampler and MaskGIT, generating a mixture of exploratory and exploitative trajectories within each group to deliberately amplify intra-group reward variance and sharpen discriminative advantage estimates. At the optimization stage, we further introduce global entropy transition anchoring (GETA) to concentrate gradient updates on the most structurally decisive decoding steps, avoiding diffuse optimization across steps of unequal importance. Extensive experiments on multiple text-to-image benchmarks validate the effectiveness of MaskSense. The contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: • We identify the visual exploration trap in MGMs, revealing that confidence-based sampling suppresses subject-token entropy before meaningful subject decisions are made, fundamentally depriving GRPO of the exploratory diversity essential to its optimization. • We propose MaskSense, a novel RL framework for MGMs that promotes diverse rollout exploration through semantic anchored routing sampling, and concentrates gradient updates on the most consequential decoding timesteps via global entropy transition anchoring. • Extensive experiments on multiple text-to-image benchmarks demonstrate that MaskSense achieves state-of-the-art performance, confirming the effectiveness of confronting the visual exploration trap for RL optimization in MGMs.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Visual Generation Models. The rapid advancement of visual generation [ 52 , 22 , 1 , 57 , 62 , 44 , 72 , 47 , 61 , 59 , 53 ] has been propelled by three dominant architectures: DMs, AR, and MGMs. DMs [ 16 , 46 , 38 , 34 , 23 , 26 ] reframe generation as an iterative denoising process, which suffers from slow inference. AR [ 49 , 7 , 33 , 11 , 58 , 9 , 66 ] predict discrete tokens sequentially via causal transformers, but their raster-order nature incurs prohibitive computational overhead at high resolution [ 37 ] . To address the limitations of both paradigms, MGMs [ 5 , 6 , 63 , 1 ] cast image synthesis as an iterative mask prediction problem, where all tokens are decoded in parallel at each step and progressively refined conditioned on previously unmasked tokens. MaskGIT [ 6 ] pioneered this direction by introducing bidirectional masked modeling with effective mask scheduling and parallel decoding, establishing the foundational framework for subsequent works. Meissonic [ 1 ] further advances this paradigm through hybrid transformer architectures and feature compression, successfully scaling masked generative modeling to high-resolution text-to-image generation. The efficiency and growing capability of MGMs motivate further exploration of their potential through RL-based optimization. Reinforcement Learning for Text-to-Image Generation. With recent advances in large language and multimodal modeling [ 73 , 74 , 20 , 19 , 56 , 27 , 43 , 50 ] , reinforcement learning (RL) [ 45 , 40 , 36 ] has proven effective in enhancing the reasoning capabilities of these models [ 17 , 71 , 8 ] , spurring its rapid adoption in text-to-image generation. Prior works primarily target preference alignment in diffusion-based models [ 51 , 4 ] , while more recent efforts successfully extend GRPO-based optimization to flow matching [ 25 , 65 , 42 ] and AR models [ 18 , 70 ] . Within MGMs, Mask-GRPO ( 28 ) formulates the iterative unmasking process as a multi-step decision-making problem and proposes transition probability to enable GRPO optimization. MaskGRPO ( 29 ) introduces modality-aware importance estimation to improve the image generation quality of multimodal discrete diffusion models. MaskFocus ( 69 ) identifies sampling steps via inter-step embedding similarity and incorporates dynamic sampling. However, none of these methods escape the confidence-based sampling strategy, leaving the visual exploration trap and principled gradient allocation across decoding steps fundamentally unaddressed as core challenges in RL optimization for MGMs.

sections.heading: 3.1 Masked Generative Models
sections.text: Masked generative models (MGMs) can be formulated as discrete diffusion processes, in which a clean token sequence x 0 x_{0} is progressively corrupted into either a new token or an absorbed state x t x_{t} at step t t via a Markov process, and a learned reverse process subsequently reconstructs the original data from these corrupted observations. Specifically, the corruption mechanism operates over discrete tokens through a transition matrix Q t {Q}_{t} , constructed as a sequential product of per-step matrices Q t = ∏ s = 1 t Q s {Q}_{t}=\prod_{s=1}^{t}{Q}_{s} . The forward process is formulated as: x t ∼ q ⁡ ( x t | x 0 , t ) , q ⁡ ( x t | x 0 , t ) = Cat ​ ( x t , x 0 ​ Q t ) x_{t}\sim q(x_{t}|x_{0},t),\quad q(x_{t}|x_{0},t)=\text{Cat}(x_{t};\,x_{0}{Q}_{t}) (1) where Q t {Q}_{t} encodes structured transition patterns, such as Gaussian kernels, nearest-neighbor mappings, or absorbing states. Meissonic adopts the absorbing state formulation, in which each token is independently replaced with a [MASK] token and remains in the absorbed state once masked. To recover the original sequence, the reverse process p θ ​ ( x t − 1 | x t ) p_{\theta}(x_{t-1}|x_{t}) is modeled by a network that learns to progressively denoise the corrupted sequence, starting from the fully masked state x T x_{T} and iteratively transitioning toward the clean data x 0 x_{0} . The reverse process is formulated as: p θ ​ ( x t − 1 | x t ) = ∑ x 0 q ⁡ ( x t − 1 | x t , x 0 ) ​ p θ ​ ( x 0 | x t ) p_{\theta}(x_{t-1}|x_{t})=\sum_{x_{0}}q(x_{t-1}|x_{t},x_{0})\,p_{\theta}(x_{0}|x_{t}) (2) During inference, generation begins from a fully [MASK] canvas and proceeds over T T iterative decoding steps [ 1 ] . At each step, the model predicts all masked tokens in parallel, commits a high-confidence subset, and remasks the remaining positions for subsequent refinement.

sections.heading: 4.1 Overview
sections.text: MaskSense addresses a fundamental mismatch in applying GRPO to masked generative models: GRPO requires diverse rollout groups, whereas confidence-based decoding in MaskGIT prematurely commits to low-uncertainty trajectories, suppressing exploration. Meanwhile, applying GRPO uniformly across all decoding steps ignores their temporally uneven contribution to generation quality. MaskSense resolves this tension via two core modules, as shown in Fig. 2 . Semantic Anchored Routing Sampling (SARS) introduces a routing strategy that integrates a novel semantic anchored sampler (SA-Sampler) alongside MaskGIT to balance exploration and exploitation, while Global Entropy Transition Anchoring (GETA) identifies the decoding timesteps with the largest entropy transition as optimization anchors, focusing GRPO updates where token commitment is most decisive.

sections.heading: 4.2 Semantic Anchored Routing Sampling
sections.text: SARS targets the visual exploration trap, in which confidence-driven decoding preferentially resolves low-uncertainty background regions while deferring commitment on semantically decisive subject tokens. To counteract this bias, SARS derives a prompt-conditioned semantic prior, injects it into the early token retention process, and routes rollout groups through a dual-branch structure. Figure 2 : Overview of MaskSense. MaskSense comprises two core modules that jointly address the visual exploration trap. At the sampling stage, SARS promotes subject-token exploration via semantic anchored decoding and sharpens advantage estimation through dual-branch rollout routing. At the optimization stage, GETA concentrates GRPO updates on critical decoding steps anchored by entropy transitions, with random remasking applied to ensure optimization diversity. We construct the semantic prior from image-to-text cross-attention cached at decoding step t t , where t ∈ { 0 , 1 , … , T } t\in\{0,1,\dots,T\} denotes the number of completed decoding steps in contrast to t t in Sec. 3 . Since early steps determine the global structure of the generated image while late-stage injection risks disrupting fine-grained detail refinement (Fig. 1 (b)), we confine semantic prior guidance to the early decoding stage via a linearly decaying temporal gate: Γ ⁡ ( t ) = max ⁡ ( 0 , 1 − r t τ ) , r t = t T \Gamma(t)=\max\!\left(0,\,1-\frac{r_{t}}{\tau}\right),\quad r_{t}=\frac{t}{T} (8) where r t r_{t} denotes the decoding progress ratio, T T is the total number of decoding steps, and τ ∈ ( 0 , 1 ] \tau\in(0,1] defines the boundary of the early decoding stage within which semantic anchoring is active. To balance exploration and exploitation within each GRPO rollout group, we stochastically partition the G G sampled trajectories for each prompt into a semantic branch 𝒢 sa \mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{sa}} (SA-Sampler) and a standard branch 𝒢 mg \mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{mg}} (MaskGIT sampler), with | 𝒢 sa | = | 𝒢 mg | = G 2 |\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{sa}}|=|\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{mg}}|=\frac{G}{2} and branch assignments fixed throughout the entire decoding process. By coupling exploratory and conservative trajectories within the same group, this design diversifies sampling outcomes, amplifies intra-group reward contrast, and yields more discriminative advantage estimates for GRPO.

sections.heading: 4.3 Global Entropy Transition Anchoring
sections.text: Even with improved rollout diversity, denoising steps contribute unevenly to policy learning: some involve only local token refinements, while others drive sharp collective uncertainty shifts that fundamentally reshape the generation trajectory, manifesting as large entropy transitions across denoising steps. GETA exploits this signal to concentrate GRPO updates on critical steps. Entropy Transition Anchor Selection. GETA measures the magnitude of change in the model’s global uncertainty across decoding steps. For each rollout, we record the token distribution at every timestep t t and compute the group-averaged entropy, formulated as: H t = − 1 G ∑ i = 1 G ∑ v ∈ 𝒱 p t i ( v ) log p t i ( v ) {H}_{t}=-\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}p^{i}_{t}(v)\log p^{i}_{t}(v) (10) where 𝒱 \mathcal{V} is the codebook and p t i ​ ( v ) p^{i}_{t}(v) is the predicted probability of token v v at step t t in the i i -th rollout. The entropy transition magnitude between consecutive steps is then computed, and the top- k k steps with the largest transitions are selected as anchor steps: Δ ​ H t = | H t + 1 − H t | , 𝒦 = topk ⁡ ( { Δ ​ H t } t = 1 T − 1 , k ) \Delta H_{t}=\left|{H}_{t+1}-{H}_{t}\right|,\quad\mathcal{K}=\mathrm{topk}\big(\{\Delta H_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T-1},k\big) (11) where 𝒦 \mathcal{K} denotes the set of selected anchor steps and k k is the number of anchor steps to select. Random Remasking for Optimization. Once the anchor set 𝒦 \mathcal{K} is obtained, we construct optimization states via random remasking [ 69 ] . Let M t traj M_{t}^{\mathrm{traj}} denote the binary mask at anchor step t t in the original rollout. Rather than replaying this, we sample a random mask M t rand M_{t}^{\mathrm{rand}} with the same mask budget: | M t rand | = | M t traj | , M t rand ∼ 𝒰 ⁡ ( { M ∈ { 0 , 1 } H × W : | M | = | M t traj | } ) , \left|M_{t}^{\mathrm{rand}}\right|=\left|M_{t}^{\mathrm{traj}}\right|,\quad M_{t}^{\mathrm{rand}}\sim\mathcal{U}\Big(\{M\in\{0,1\}^{H\times W}:\ |M|=\left|M_{t}^{\mathrm{traj}}\right|\}\Big), (12) where 𝒰 ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \mathcal{U}(\cdot) denotes the uniform distribution, H × W H\times W is the spatial resolution of the latent token map. This random mask is then applied to the final generated latent x T x_{T} to produce the remasked input: x ~ t = M t rand ⊙ [ MASK ] + ( 1 − M t rand ) ⊙ x T , \tilde{x}_{t}=M_{t}^{\mathrm{rand}}\odot[\texttt{MASK}]+\left(1-M_{t}^{\mathrm{rand}}\right)\odot x_{T}, (13) where ⊙ \odot denotes element-wise product. By decoupling optimization from the exact trajectory mask pattern while preserving the number of masked positions, the policy is trained around each critical transition without overfitting to any single realized masking configuration. The remasked input x ~ t \tilde{x}_{t} is subsequently used to compute the importance ratio r t i ​ ( θ ) r_{t}^{i}(\theta) in Eq. 5 , and the GRPO objective (Eq. 4 ) is optimized exclusively over the selected anchor steps t ∈ 𝒦 t\in\mathcal{K} : 𝒥 MaskSense ​ ( θ ) = M t rand ⊙ 𝒥 GRPO ​ ( θ ) | t ∈ 𝒦 , \mathcal{J}_{\text{MaskSense}}(\theta)=M_{t}^{\mathrm{rand}}\odot\,\mathcal{J}_{\text{GRPO}}(\theta)\big|_{t\in\mathcal{K}}, (14) where the mask M t rand M_{t}^{\mathrm{rand}} restricts gradient updates to the masked positions of the remasked input x ~ t \tilde{x}_{t} , ensuring that only the tokens requiring prediction contribute to the optimization objective. sections.heading: 5.1 Experimental Setup
sections.text: Training Settings. All experiments are conducted on Meissonic [ 1 ] , a masked text-to-image model at 1024 × 1024 1024\times 1024 resolution, trained on 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs. Following the standard masked-generation RL setup [ 69 ] , we adopt a classifier-free guidance scale of 5 5 during both training and inference, perform 64 iterative decoding steps, and set the number of selected optimization anchors to 6. For the compositional image generation task [ 12 ] , we use 50K GenEval-style prompts sourced from Flow-GRPO [ 25 ] . For preference alignment, we use 10K training samples from HPS v2 dataset [ 60 ] . More implementation details are provided in Appendix A . Evaluation Details. We evaluate MaskSense from two complementary perspectives: (i) task-specific accuracy on in-distribution test sets, which directly measures the model’s ability to handle the target task. (ii) general image quality on DrawBench [ 39 ] , which assesses broader generalization beyond the training distribution. The latter is quantified using a comprehensive set of metrics, including image quality (DeQA [ 68 ] ) and human preference scores (PickScore [ 21 ] , ImageReward [ 64 ] ). sections.heading: 5.2 Main Results
sections.text: Quantitative Comparison. Tab. 1 and 3 demonstrate that MaskSense achieves superior performance across both tasks, improving GenEval by 0.32 and HPS by 7.50 over the Meissonic baseline. Furthermore, these gains generalize beyond the training reward domain, as MaskSense achieves the best scores across DrawBench metrics, confirming broader generalization. As shown in Fig. 3 , MaskSense exhibits superior training stability and faster convergence to a higher final performance. Qualitative Comparison. Fig. 4 provides qualitative evidence consistent with the quantitative results. MaskSense produces richer fine-grained details, complex textures, and higher visual fidelity for preference-oriented prompts, while other methods yield flatter appearance and incomplete stylistic rendering. For compositional prompts, MaskSense more reliably satisfies object-level constraints including count, spatial arrangement, and color attribution, demonstrating significant advantages of MaskSense in aligning with target preferences. sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We present MaskSense to address the visual exploration trap in masked generative models, where confidence-based sampling prematurely suppresses subject-token diversity and undermines the effectiveness of GRPO optimization. By anchoring subject tokens during early decoding via semantic priors, MaskSense preserves the high-entropy exploration space that confidence-based sampling would otherwise collapse, enabling sharper intra-group advantage estimation through dual-branch rollout routing. Building on the enriched rollout diversity, MaskSense further identifies timesteps of maximal entropy transition as optimization anchors to address the uneven contribution of individual steps to policy learning, concentrating gradient updates where token commitment is most decisive. Extensive experiments demonstrate the gains achieved by MaskSense and validate the critical role of confronting the visual exploration trap for RL optimization in masked generative models.

sections.heading: A.1 Dataset and Reward
sections.text: Dataset. For the compositional image generation task, 50K prompts are constructed using the official GenEval [ 12 ] scripts, following Flow-GRPO [ 25 ] , covering six sub-tasks with the prompt sampling ratio set to Position : Counting : Attribute Binding : Colors : Two Objects : Single Object = 7 : 5 : 3 : 1 : 1 : 0. The same dataset is also used for multi-reward joint optimization. For human preference alignment, we use 10K training samples from the HPS v2 dataset [ 60 ] , a large-scale benchmark collecting pairwise human judgments over generated images across diverse prompt styles. We further evaluate out-of-distribution generalization on DrawBench [ 39 ] , a benchmark comprising 200 prompts across 11 diverse categories that probes broad generative capabilities beyond the training distribution. Reward. For compositional image generation, we adopt the GenEval reward, which is computed based on rule-based detection of object presence, count, spatial position, and color attribution. For human preference alignment, we employ the HPS [ 60 ] reward model. For multi-reward joint optimization, we simultaneously optimize GenEval and CLIP [ 35 ] rewards.

sections.heading: A.2 Implementation Details
sections.text: Training. All experiments are conducted on Meissonic [ 1 ] , a masked text-to-image model at 1024 × 1024 1024\times 1024 resolution, trained on 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs. We use the AdamW optimizer with a learning rate of 2 × 10 − 6 2\times 10^{-6} . The maximum prompt length and completion length are set to 512 and 1024, respectively, with a sampling temperature of 1.0 1.0 . For GRPO optimization, we set the group size to G = 8 G=8 , with a per-device batch size of 1 and gradient accumulation steps of 1. Following the standard masked-generation RL setup [ 69 ] , we adopt a classifier-free guidance scale of 5 during both training and inference, and perform 64 iterative decoding steps. The number of selected optimization anchors is set to k = 6 k=6 , and the KL penalty coefficient is set to β = 0.01 \beta=0.01 . For SARS, the semantic guidance strength is set to λ = 0.5 \lambda=0.5 and the temporal gate threshold to τ = 0.5 \tau=0.5 . Evaluation. For compositional image generation, we evaluate on the GenEval benchmark [ 12 ] using its official evaluation pipeline, which detects object bounding boxes and colors and infers their spatial relations. The evaluation set comprises 553 prompts, for each of which we generate 4 images to ensure stable and reliable score estimation. For human preference alignment, we evaluate on a held-out test set of 400 prompts from HPS v2 [ 60 ] . For out-of-distribution generalization, we evaluate on DrawBench [ 39 ] , a benchmark of 200 prompts spanning 11 diverse categories, generating 5 images per prompt to ensure broader coverage and stable generalization assessment. To ensure fairness and stability during evaluation, all models are assessed using the original MaskGIT sampler as the decoding strategy at evaluation time, regardless of the sampling strategy employed during training. The proposed SA-Sampler is exclusively utilized during the RL training phase to promote exploratory diversity in rollout generation and is not applied at evaluation time. All quantitative results reported in the main paper are obtained under the above evaluation protocol. To ensure statistical reliability, all metrics are averaged over multiple generated images per prompt, which reduces variance and yields more stable estimates across different random seeds, ensuring that the reported numbers reflect the model’s generative capability rather than individual sampling artifacts.

sections.heading: A.3 Quality Metrics
sections.text: The details of task accuracy metrics and quality metrics are as follows: • GenEval [ 12 ] : An object-focused evaluation framework that benchmarks T2I models on six compositional image generation tasks. The official pipeline detects object bounding boxes and colors and infers spatial relations between them. Rewards follow rule-based criteria: (i) Counting: r = 1 − | N g ​ e ​ n − N r ​ e ​ f | / N r ​ e ​ f r=1-|N_{gen}-N_{ref}|/N_{ref} ; (ii) Position / Color: a partial reward is granted when the object count is correct, with the remainder awarded upon correct prediction of position or color. • HPS [ 60 ] : A scoring model obtained by fine-tuning CLIP [ 35 ] on the Human Preference Dataset v2 (HPD v2), a large-scale collection of 798K pairwise human preference annotations over images generated from diverse prompts and models. HPS v2 predicts the likelihood that a generated image will be preferred by humans, serving as a reliable proxy for aesthetic quality and text-image alignment. • DeQA [ 68 ] : A multimodal large language model-based image quality assessment metric that estimates overall perceptual quality by accounting for distortions, texture degradation, and AI-specific artifacts, trained via a fidelity loss over soft score distributions. • PickScore [ 21 ] : A preference scoring model fine-tuned from CLIP [ 35 ] on Pick-a-Pic, a large-scale dataset of real user preference choices between pairs of images generated from identical prompts, providing judgments strongly aligned with human evaluation across text-image alignment and visual aesthetics. • ImageReward [ 64 ] : The first general-purpose reward model for text-to-image generation, trained to capture human preference dimensions encompassing text-image alignment, perceptual fidelity, and harmlessness. sections.heading: Appendix B Limitations and Societal Impacts
sections.text: Limitations. While our method demonstrates strong performance across multiple benchmarks, several limitations remain. First, the proposed reinforcement learning framework is grounded in the general MaskGIT paradigm, which is adopted by the vast majority of existing masked generative models as their core sampling strategy. It is therefore in principle compatible with a broad family of such models. Validating and extending its application to a wider range of base architectures [ 67 ] will be one of the primary focuses of our future work. Second, the current work focuses solely on image generation, leaving the exploration of reinforcement learning for multi-modal discrete diffusion models to future work, including the analysis of sampling and optimization across different modalities toward a unified RL framework for multi-modal masked generative models [ 63 ] . Societal Impacts. This work aims to advance text-to-image generation by aligning masked generative models with human preferences and compositional understanding. The proposed framework has the potential to benefit a wide range of creative, educational, and industrial applications. However, improved generative capabilities may also be exploited to produce misleading or harmful visual content, raising concerns about misinformation and malicious use. Additionally, as the model is trained on large-scale data, it may inadvertently inherit and amplify societal biases present in the training corpus. We encourage responsible deployment of the proposed method and hope to inspire future research on safety, fairness, and interpretability in generative modeling.

Fig. 8 and 9 illustrate the sampling trajectories of the MaskGIT sampler and SA-Sampler across diverse prompt categories, including abstract art, natural landscapes, character portraits, architectural scenes, and still-life compositions. In contrast, the SA-Sampler, without any modification to the model parameters, redirects early token commitment toward semantically critical subject regions, enabling the discovery of higher-quality generative trajectories through broader subject-space exploration. Learn more × Back to arXiv License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.17009v1 [cs.CV] 12 Oct 2026 MaskSense: Confronting the Visual Exploration Trap in Masked Image Generation Yawen Shao † † thanks: ˜Work done at Tongyi Lab. Affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China Affiliation: Tongyi Lab, Alibaba Group Jie Xiao Affiliation: Tongyi Lab, Alibaba Group Kai Zhu † † thanks: ˜Corresponding author. Affiliation: Tongyi Lab, Alibaba Group Yu Liu Affiliation: Tongyi Lab, Alibaba Group Hongchen Luo Affiliation: Northeastern University Xueyang Fu Affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China Yang Cao Affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China Wei Zhai 2 2 footnotemark: 2 Affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China Zheng-Jun Zha Affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China Abstract Reinforcement learning (RL) has shown strong potential for aligning generative models with human intent, but adapting RL to masked generative models (MGMs) remains largely underexplored. Existing approaches that directly adapt Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to MGMs leave a foundational conflict unaddressed: MGMs’ exploitative decoding nature is inherently at odds with the exploratory diversity that GRPO presupposes. In this work, we reveal a structural decoding bias termed the visual exploration trap : confidence-based sampling trades the exploration of diverse subject realizations for the greedy resolution of low-uncertainty background regions, causing premature collapse of the generative exploration space and starving GRPO of the rollout diversity it depends on. To this end, we propose MaskSense , a novel RL framework for MGMs that confronts the visual exploration trap at both the sampling and optimization stages. Specifically, we introduce a semantic anchored routing sampling mechanism that leverages semantic priors to preserve high-entropy subject token exploration while amplifying intra-group reward variance through exploratory-exploitative routing to yield more discriminative advantage estimates. Furthermore, we design a global entropy transition anchoring strategy to identify the most consequential decoding steps and concentrate gradient updates on them. Extensive experiments on multiple text-to-image benchmarks demonstrate that MaskSense substantially improves upon the base model, with GenEval accuracy improving from 54% to 86% and HPS from 28.89 to 36.39, achieving state-of-the-art performance. 1 Introduction Masked generative models (MGMs) [ 1 , 5 , 63 , 15 ] have recently emerged as a compelling paradigm for visual synthesis, challenging the long-standing dominance of autoregressive models (AR) [ 57 , 24 , 48 ] and diffusion models (DMs) [ 46 , 16 , 23 ] by reformulating image generation as iterative masked token prediction. Central to this paradigm is the confidence-based sampling strategy of MaskGIT [ 6 ] , which predicts all masked tokens in parallel at each step and retains only the most confident subset while remasking the remainder for subsequent iterations, making the decoding process exploitative. Reinforcement learning (RL) [ 45 , 40 , 36 ] has proven highly effective in enhancing the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) [ 13 , 17 , 54 , 41 ] , while its application to MGMs remains comparatively underexplored relative to diffusion models [ 25 , 42 , 65 ] and AR models [ 18 , 70 ] . Recent works [ 69 , 28 ] have begun addressing this gap by applying Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to MGMs, yet retain the confidence-based sampler as a fixed component with minimal adaptation to the masked generation setting. This overlooks a fundamental prerequisite of GRPO: its effectiveness derives from group-relative advantage estimation, which presupposes rollouts sufficiently diverse to cover meaningful regions of the solution space, a requirement inherently at odds with the exploitative nature of confidence-based sampling. In this paper, we identify and characterize precisely how this conflict manifests as a structural bias that we term the visual exploration trap . Specifically, tokens with lower uncertainty predominantly correspond to simple background textures in natural images [ 30 ] , causing background regions to be committed well before semantically critical subject areas are ever explored (Fig. 1 (a)). Subject tokens, by contrast, retain high predictive entropy throughout the early generation steps, while their fixation ratio remains near zero (Fig. 1 (c)), indicating that substantial generative diversity is available yet remains entirely unexploited. By the time subject tokens begin to be retained after step 20, the surrounding background context has been largely committed, severely narrowing the space of potential generative branches [ 32 , 54 ] and limiting the diversity and quality of the resulting subject regions [ 30 ] . The originally high entropy of subject tokens is thus suppressed before any meaningful subject decision is made, as the model effectively sacrifices diverse subject realizations to greedily resolve low-uncertainty background regions, directly undermining the rollout diversity that GRPO requires. This trap necessitates a rethink of RL for MGMs. Figure 1 : Motivation. (a) MaskGIT keeps subject tokens masked while committing background regions early, whereas SA-Sampler resolves subject regions earlier via semantic anchoring. (b) SA-Sampler consistently discovers higher-reward trajectories through broader generative exploration. (c) SA-Sampler maintains higher subject-token fixation ratios and elevated entropy, effectively escaping the visual exploration trap. To tackle this challenge, we propose MaskSense (Fig. 2 ), a novel RL framework designed for MGMs that directly confronts the visual exploration trap at both the sampling and optimization stages. At the sampling stage, we propose the semantic anchored routing sampling (SARS) mechanism, built upon the Semantic Anchored Sampler (SA-Sampler), which employs semantic priors to anchor subject tokens during the early generation steps (Fig. 1 (a)). This design preserves the high-entropy exploration space that confidence-based sampling would otherwise suppress (Fig. 1 (c)), enabling the discovery of higher-reward trajectories through broader generative exploration (Fig. 1 (b)). SARS further routes rollouts stochastically between SA-Sampler and MaskGIT, generating a mixture of exploratory and exploitative trajectories within each group to deliberately amplify intra-group reward variance and sharpen discriminative advantage estimates. At the optimization stage, we further introduce global entropy transition anchoring (GETA) to concentrate gradient updates on the most structurally decisive decoding steps, avoiding diffuse optimization across steps of unequal importance. Extensive experiments on multiple text-to-image benchmarks validate the effectiveness of MaskSense. The contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: • We identify the visual exploration trap in MGMs, revealing that confidence-based sampling suppresses subject-token entropy before meaningful subject decisions are made, fundamentally depriving GRPO of the exploratory diversity essential to its optimization. • We propose MaskSense, a novel RL framework for MGMs that promotes diverse rollout exploration through semantic anchored routing sampling, and concentrates gradient updates on the most consequential decoding timesteps via global entropy transition anchoring. • Extensive experiments on multiple text-to-image benchmarks demonstrate that MaskSense achieves state-of-the-art performance, confirming the effectiveness of confronting the visual exploration trap for RL optimization in MGMs. 2 Related Work Visual Generation Models. The rapid advancement of visual generation [ 52 , 22 , 1 , 57 , 62 , 44 , 72 , 47 , 61 , 59 , 53 ] has been propelled by three dominant architectures: DMs, AR, and MGMs. DMs [ 16 , 46 , 38 , 34 , 23 , 26 ] reframe generation as an iterative denoising process, which suffers from slow inference. AR [ 49 , 7 , 33 , 11 , 58 , 9 , 66 ] predict discrete tokens sequentially via causal transformers, but their raster-order nature incurs prohibitive computational overhead at high resolution [ 37 ] . To address the limitations of both paradigms, MGMs [ 5 , 6 , 63 , 1 ] cast image synthesis as an iterative mask prediction problem, where all tokens are decoded in parallel at each step and progressively refined conditioned on previously unmasked tokens. MaskGIT [ 6 ] pioneered this direction by introducing bidirectional masked modeling with effective mask scheduling and parallel decoding, establishing the foundational framework for subsequent works. Meissonic [ 1 ] further advances this paradigm through hybrid transformer architectures and feature compression, successfully scaling masked generative modeling to high-resolution text-to-image generation. The efficiency and growing capability of MGMs motivate further exploration of their potential through RL-based optimization. Reinforcement Learning for Text-to-Image Generation. With recent advances in large language and multimodal modeling [ 73 , 74 , 20 , 19 , 56 , 27 , 43 , 50 ] , reinforcement learning (RL) [ 45 , 40 , 36 ] has proven effective in enhancing the reasoning capabilities of these models [ 17 , 71 , 8 ] , spurring its rapid adoption in text-to-image generation. Prior works primarily target preference alignment in diffusion-based models [ 51 , 4 ] , while more recent efforts successfully extend GRPO-based optimization to flow matching [ 25 , 65 , 42 ] and AR models [ 18 , 70 ] . Within MGMs, Mask-GRPO ( 28 ) formulates the iterative unmasking process as a multi-step decision-making problem and proposes transition probability to enable GRPO optimization. MaskGRPO ( 29 ) introduces modality-aware importance estimation to improve the image generation quality of multimodal discrete diffusion models. MaskFocus ( 69 ) identifies sampling steps via inter-step embedding similarity and incorporates dynamic sampling. However, none of these methods escape the confidence-based sampling strategy, leaving the visual exploration trap and principled gradient allocation across decoding steps fundamentally unaddressed as core challenges in RL optimization for MGMs. 3 Preliminaries 3.1 Masked Generative Models Masked generative models (MGMs) can be formulated as discrete diffusion processes, in which a clean token sequence x 0 x_{0} is progressively corrupted into either a new token or an absorbed state x t x_{t} at step t t via a Markov process, and a learned reverse process subsequently reconstructs the original data from these corrupted observations. Meanwhile, applying GRPO uniformly across all decoding steps ignores their temporally uneven contribution to generation quality. MaskSense resolves this tension via two core modules, as shown in Fig. 2 . Semantic Anchored Routing Sampling (SARS) introduces a routing strategy that integrates a novel semantic anchored sampler (SA-Sampler) alongside MaskGIT to balance exploration and exploitation, while Global Entropy Transition Anchoring (GETA) identifies the decoding timesteps with the largest entropy transition as optimization anchors, focusing GRPO updates where token commitment is most decisive. 4.2 Semantic Anchored Routing Sampling SARS targets the visual exploration trap, in which confidence-driven decoding preferentially resolves low-uncertainty background regions while deferring commitment on semantically decisive subject tokens. To counteract this bias, SARS derives a prompt-conditioned semantic prior, injects it into the early token retention process, and routes rollout groups through a dual-branch structure. At the sampling stage, SARS promotes subject-token exploration via semantic anchored decoding and sharpens advantage estimation through dual-branch rollout routing. At the optimization stage, GETA concentrates GRPO updates on critical decoding steps anchored by entropy transitions, with random remasking applied to ensure optimization diversity. Semantic Prior Construction. Jointly normalizing MaskGIT and SA-Sampler trajectories can introduce a branch-dependent component, motivating us to distinguish cross-branch contrast from trajectory-level quality. Let b i ∈ { MG , SA } b_{i}\in\{\mathrm{MG},\mathrm{SA}\} denote the branch of rollout i i , and let μ b \mu_{b} and μ \mu be the branch-wise and pooled reward means. The centered reward decomposes as R i − μ = ( R i − μ b i ) + ( μ b i − μ ) R_{i}-\mu=(R_{i}-\mu_{b_{i}})+(\mu_{b_{i}}-\mu) , where the two terms capture within-branch trajectory quality and cross-branch reward contrast, respectively. We remove the latter mean-offset term using branch-conditioned normalization within each G = 8 G=8 rollout group, which enforces 𝔼 ⁡ [ A ^ i ∣ b i = SA ] = 𝔼 ⁡ [ A ^ i ∣ b i = MG ] = 0 . \mathbb{E}\!\left[\hat{A}_{i}\mid b_{i}=\mathrm{SA}\right]=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\hat{A}_{i}\mid b_{i}=\mathrm{MG}\right]=0. Dual-branch training still outperforms MaskGIT-only + + GETA (36.08 vs. 35.64 HPS), while pooled normalization reaches 36.39, showing that cross-branch contrast contributes to, but does not account for, the overall gain. A 300-prompt overlap analysis further supports this conclusion: the branch reward ranges overlap for 90.7% of prompts, with 26.9% of SA-Sampler rollouts below the pooled mean and 25.7% of MaskGIT rollouts above it. Thus, sampler identity does not determine the advantage sign. Since all variants use MaskGIT for evaluation, the observed gain stems from the learned policy itself. Effect of Global Entropy Transition Anchoring. We compare GETA against random early-step selection and similarity-based selection [ 69 ] in Fig. 5 (b). Although restricting anchors to the first 10% or 20% of steps brings faster initial gains, it ultimately leads to training collapse, possibly due to highly masked states inducing unstable optimization targets. Similarity-based selection appears more stable initially but exhibits increasing instability in later stages, as embedding similarity captures visual representational change but fails to align with the model’s most decisive policy decision points. As shown in Fig. 6 , the top row exhibits dominant transitions spread across the first 30 steps where each committed decision critically shapes the overall image structure, while the bottom row concentrates transitions within the first 10 steps with later steps contributing only minor detail refinement. This prompt-adaptive distribution of critical steps validates the rationality of GETA’s entropy-guided anchor selection. These reward-independent evaluations confirm improvements in both compositional faithfulness and perceptual quality. 6 Conclusion We present MaskSense to address the visual exploration trap in masked generative models, where confidence-based sampling prematurely suppresses subject-token diversity and undermines the effectiveness of GRPO optimization. By anchoring subject tokens during early decoding via semantic priors, MaskSense preserves the high-entropy exploration space that confidence-based sampling would otherwise collapse, enabling sharper intra-group advantage estimation through dual-branch rollout routing. Building on the enriched rollout diversity, MaskSense further identifies timesteps of maximal entropy transition as optimization anchors to address the uneven contribution of individual steps to policy learning, concentrating gradient updates where token commitment is most decisive. Extensive experiments demonstrate the gains achieved by MaskSense and validate the critical role of confronting the visual exploration trap for RL optimization in masked generative models.
